strings.hist.soviet.propiska.title: Internal passport and propiska
strings.hist.soviet.propiska.text: On 27 December 1932 the Soviet Union introduced a uniform internal passport with compulsory registration, the propiska. Anyone living in towns, workers’ settlements and border zones needed a passport from the age of sixteen, bearing the militia’s registration stamp. Without a propiska there was no housing, no work and no study; anyone refused registration had to leave the place. The passport regulations of 1940 allowed stricter rules for capitals, border areas and important railway junctions. Collective farmers received no passport and could leave their village only with the permission of the kolkhoz chairman or the village soviet. Only the passport regulations of 28 August 1974 included them; their passports were issued from 1976 to 1981. In Russia the propiska was abolished in 1993.
strings.hist.soviet.foreign_correspondents.title: Correspondents in Moscow
strings.hist.soviet.foreign_correspondents.text: Until 1961 Western correspondents in Moscow had to hand in every report in writing at the counter of the Central Telegraph Office. Behind it worked censors from the Glavlit authority, whom no correspondent ever got to see; only after their approval did the text go to the editors. In March 1961 the Foreign Ministry’s press chief, Mikhail Kharlamov, announced the end of this pre-censorship: reports could now be telephoned from anywhere, but copies had to be kept ready. The control remained. Interviews went through the ministry’s press department, and trips more than 40 kilometres outside Moscow had to be registered in advance. Anyone who displeased was expelled – in August 1961, for example, the West German correspondent Botho Kirsch – or was not allowed back in after leave.
strings.hist.reich.schriftleitergesetz.title: The Editors Law
strings.hist.reich.schriftleitergesetz.text: With the Editors Law of 4 October 1933, in force from 1 January 1934, journalism became a state-licensed profession. Anyone who wanted to write for a newspaper needed to be entered on the register of the Reich Press Chamber, to hold German Reich citizenship and to prove “Aryan” descent, for their spouse as well. Section 14 obliged editors to keep out anything that might weaken the strength of the Reich or the “will of the community”. They were answerable to the state, no longer to the publisher. Around 1,300 journalists lost their jobs. From July 1933 the Propaganda Ministry laid down at the daily Reich Press Conference what was to be written; by 1945 there were an estimated 80,000 to 100,000 directives, which were to be destroyed after use.
strings.hist.reich.blockleiter.title: Block and cell leaders
strings.hist.reich.blockleiter.text: In the cities an NSDAP block leader was responsible for 40 to 60 households, around 170 people; four to eight blocks formed a cell. At the start of 1935 there were over 210,000 block leaders, almost half a million with their helpers, and four times as many by 1939. They collected dues, distributed propaganda and kept a household card index, one card per household. Their information was turned into “political assessments” for job applications, for the surveillance of released prisoners and for Gestapo investigations. The block leader was not a policeman, but together with the police and registration offices he also registered the Jewish neighbours. In a sample of files from the Düsseldorf Gestapo, 30 per cent of cases originated from tip-offs by other agencies, party offices included.
